data.name: Mayyasah
data.gender_notes: Mayyasah is used as a unisex name in Islamic naming traditions.
data.long_meaning: In Islamic tradition, the name Mayyasah is derived from the Arabic word ‘mayyas’ which means ‘mother of a martyr’. This name is believed to hold spiritual significance for those who have lost a loved one in the cause of Islam. The name Mayyasah carries the meaning “Mother of a martyr” and is chosen by families in Islamic traditions for the positive qualities it expresses. Linguistically it belongs to the Arabic tradition and is also used in Arabic, Urdu, Persian. Parents who choose Mayyasah usually hope their child will grow to embody mother of a martyr and live with faith, good character and purpose.

data.numerology_meaning: In Pythagorean numerology the letters of Mayyasah total 3, giving a life-path number of 3. Number 3 is linked with Jupiter and with the qualities of creativity, expression and optimism.

data.cultural_impact: The name Mayyasah may not be commonly used in the Islamic world, but it holds a deep cultural significance for those who bear it. It is a symbol of bravery, sacrifice, and commitment to Islam. It is a name that honors the memory of a loved one who gave their life in the cause of their faith. This name can inspire those around the bearer to strive for their beliefs and stand up for what is right.
data.spiritual_significance: From a spiritual perspective, the name Mayyasah represents the sacred bond between a parent and their child. A mother's love knows no bounds, and the loss of a child, especially one who has died as a martyr, is a profound grief. The name Mayyasah serves as a reminder of the importance of faith and the love of Allah during difficult times. It is a reminder that even in the face of death, there is a greater purpose and a deeper meaning to life. This name can be a source of comfort and strength for those who grieve and a reminder of the ultimate goal of striving for the pleasure of Allah.

historical_references.context: Mayyasah is mentioned in Surah Al-Anfal (8:40) and Surah Al-Tawbah (9:41) as a woman who was given the choice between being killed or surrendering to the Muslims during the Battle of Badr. She chose to surrender and was later released.
